JSON: Name: sleep_apnea_carepathway_education_adherence Title: Longitudinal survey-based causal analysis of how structured patient education and clinic characteristics affect diagnostic delay and CPAP adherence in obstructive sleep apnea care pathways Short Hypothesis: Provision of structured patient education and guidance at the start of therapy causally increases CPAP adherence at six months, measured as higher mean nightly use (hours) and a larger proportion of patients achieving ≥4 hours per night. Related Work: Existing work characterizes obstructive sleep apnea epidemiology, device efficacy, and adherence correlates, and compares PSG versus home PG diagnostics. Prior studies document large increases in diagnoses and treatment modalities (CPAP, MAD, SPT, hypoglossal stimulation) and report cross-sectional associations between adherence and factors such as daytime symptoms, comfort, and follow-up support. Limitations in the prior literature include: focus on physiological endpoints (AHI) rather than patient-reported outcomes and care-pathway metrics; reliance on single-center or short-term datasets; sparse causal analyses of the effect of education/guidance or home care provider interaction on long-term adherence; inconsistent measurement and reporting across clinics of education intensity, multidisciplinary availability, and follow-up frequency; and limited national-scale longitudinal comparisons between clinic practices (PSG/PG use, throughput, multidisciplinary teams) and patient outcomes. Gaps remain in quantifying modifiable clinic-level and process-level drivers of diagnostic delay, treatment choice, and sustained adherence using large repeated-survey data. Abstract: Timely diagnosis and sustained adherence to therapy are central to improving health outcomes for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), yet national-scale evidence linking care-pathway processes to patient adherence and health gains is limited. This study will use 2005–2020 annual patient and sleep-clinic survey datasets to estimate the causal effect of structured education and guidance at treatment initiation on CPAP adherence and self-reported health improvement. We combine multilevel regression, propensity-score methods, and difference-in-differences analyses to control for patient case-mix, clinic characteristics, and temporal policy changes. The main contribution is a quantified, risk-adjusted estimate of how variation in education intensity, home care provider contact, and multidisciplinary clinic capacity affects time-to-diagnosis, mean nightly CPAP use, and the proportion of patients meeting adherence thresholds at six months. Expected outcomes include identification of the strongest modifiable process levers in the care pathway, provision of benchmarks for clinic performance, and empirical evidence to inform guideline and reimbursement decisions focused on patient-centered outcomes. Experiments: Datasets: annual ApneuVereniging patient surveys (2005–2020, aggregated n≈2.7k–5.2k/year), sleep-clinic surveys (2005–2020, all Dutch sleep clinics), national device prescription counts and registry summaries. Preprocess: harmonize variables across years, map education/guidance into an ordinal intensity score (none, minimal, structured session(s), ongoing home-care support), derive outcome variables: mean nightly CPAP use (hours), percent of nights ≥4h, treatment persistence (days/week), change in self-rated health (post minus pre), time-to-diagnosis (years). Baselines: (1) unadjusted group comparison (received structured education vs not); (2) multivariable mixed-effects regression with patient and clinic random intercepts excluding education variable; (3) multivariable regression including education variable. Primary analysis: estimate average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) of structured education using propensity score matching (covariates: age, sex, BMI, baseline symptoms, AHI where available, comorbidities, initial sleep-study type, year, clinic throughput). Secondary causal checks: instrumental variable analysis using clinic-level availability of multidisciplinary teams or mandated education programs as instruments; difference-in-differences exploiting policy inclusion years for MAD/SPT if applicable. Models: hierarchical linear models for continuous outcomes, logistic mixed models for binary adherence thresholds, survival models for time-to-diagnosis. Ablations: (A) remove home care provider contact variable; (B) restrict to PSG-confirmed cases; (C) restrict to new diagnoses post-2010; (D) compare models with objective device-derived adherence (where available) versus self-report. Evaluation metrics: mean difference in nightly hours (primary), odds ratio for achieving ≥4h/night, mean change in self-rated health, hazard ratio for time-to-diagnosis; report 95% confidence intervals, p-values, and standardized effect sizes. Robustness: multiple imputation for missing covariates, sensitivity analysis for unobserved confounding (E-value), cross-validated predictive performance for adherence models. Predefine significance threshold alpha=0.05 and preregister analysis plan. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data quality and measurement: reliance on self-reported survey responses and changes in survey instruments across years can introduce measurement error and noncomparable variables. Selection bias: patient surveys are from a patient association membership and may not represent the full OSA population; clinic surveys may have differential nonresponse. Confounding: residual confounding by unobserved factors (motivation, socioeconomic status, local referral practices) may bias causal estimates; instrument validity may be weak if clinic-level instruments correlate with unobserved determinants of adherence. Temporal policy and technology changes: evolving reimbursement, introduction of MAD/SPT/hypoglossal stimulation, and COVID-19 disruptions (2020) complicate interpretation of longitudinal trends. Generalizability: findings based on Dutch care pathways and insurance context may not transfer to other healthcare systems. Outcome limitations: MAD adherence and health effect measurement are less standardized than CPAP device telemetry; objective adherence data availability may be limited. Computational: complex hierarchical and causal models require careful tuning and sufficient sample sizes within strata; small subgroup sizes (e.g., PSG-only clinics) limit power for some comparisons.
